title: Trade is being reorganised by geopolitics, services, green rules, and food-security dependence, with smaller economies bearing more adaptation costs
source_unit: United Nations Trade and Development, Global Trade Update (January 2026): Top trends redefining global trade in 2026
geography: Global trade, developing economies excluding China, least developed countries, global value chains, services, food and fertilizer markets, and trade regulation

observations.period: 2025-2026 projected; global growth, trade demand, and developing-economy exposure

global_growth_2026.unit: percent projected global economic growth in 2026, approximately

developing_growth_excluding_china_2026.unit: percent projected growth for developing economies excluding China in 2026, approximately

trade_environment.value: slower growth, geopolitical fragmentation, digital and green transitions, and tighter national regulations are reshaping trade flows and value chains

development_constraint.value: slower demand and tighter financial conditions can limit infrastructure and industrialisation investment in developing economies

observations.method: UN Trade and Development synthesis of global trade, growth, policy, sector, value-chain, and developing-economy trends for 2026.
observations.uncertainty: Forecasts are scenario-sensitive and do not establish country-specific welfare, employment, firm survival, household prices, or realized trade-policy effects.
observations.subgroup: Developing and developed economies, exporters and importers, small firms, workers, households exposed to food and manufactured-goods prices, and governments managing trade and industrial policy.
observations.counterinterpretation: Slower global demand can still create openings through regional diversification, South–South trade, services, and targeted industrial upgrading; exposure varies sharply by sector and country.

denominator.unit: global trade in goods, services, and value-chain-linked flows

value_chain_trade_share.unit: percent of global trade occurring within value chains being reshaped by geopolitics, industrial policy, and new technologies, approximately

services_share_global_trade.unit: percent of global trade represented by services

services_export_growth_2025.unit: percent growth in services exports in 2025, approximately

digitally_deliverable_constraint.value: digitally deliverable services are growing rapidly but remain limited in least developed countries

observations.method: UN Trade and Development comparison of value-chain flows, goods and services trade, digitally deliverable services, and country-group participation.
observations.uncertainty: Trade shares and growth rates do not show who captures value, the quality of jobs, local tax revenue, labor bargaining power, or whether digital access is affordable and reliable.
observations.subgroup: Manufacturing and service firms, logistics and digital-infrastructure providers, workers, consumers of traded services, least developed countries, and governments seeking diversification.
observations.counterinterpretation: Services growth can widen participation and reduce dependence on physical trade routes, while relocation and supplier diversification may create new entry points for peripheral economies.

observations.period: 1995-2025; South–South trade and changing development pathways

denominator.unit: developing-country merchandise exports and destination markets

south_south_exports_2025.unit: US dollars of South–South merchandise exports in 2025, approximately

south_south_exports_1995.unit: US dollars of South–South merchandise exports in 1995, approximately

developing_exports_to_developing_markets.unit: percent of developing-country exports going to other developing markets

regional_value_chain_signal.value: Asia leads South–South trade growth, while Africa and Latin America are strengthening interregional links

observations.method: UN Trade and Development historical and current comparison of developing-country merchandise exports and destination composition.
observations.uncertainty: Trade growth does not automatically imply inclusive development, local value capture, improved labor conditions, or reduced geopolitical dependence; commodity and manufacturing composition differ across regions.
observations.subgroup: Developing-country exporters, regional producers, logistics systems, workers, consumers, and governments negotiating market access and industrial upgrading.
observations.counterinterpretation: South–South trade can diversify demand and strengthen bargaining options, but it can also reproduce asymmetries if value chains, finance, technology, or standards remain concentrated.

observations.period: 2020-2026; regulation, food security, and resource-transition pressure

denominator.unit: global trade measures, commodity exports, and trade-regulation exposure

new_discriminatory_trade_measures_since_.unit: new discriminatory trade measures introduced globally since 2020, approximately

technical_regulation_trade_share.unit: percent of global trade affected by technical regulations, approximately

food_products_commodity_exports.unit: percent of commodity exports represented by food products, approximately

food_security_pressures.value: high fertilizer prices and climate shocks threaten supplies while many developing countries depend on imports for basic needs

rules_expanding.value: environmental, social, and security-driven trade rules are expected to expand in 2026

observations.method: UN Trade and Development synthesis of trade-policy inventories, technical regulations, agricultural trade dependence, fertilizer conditions, climate risks, and sustainability-related rules.
observations.uncertainty: Counts of measures do not identify implementation, sector-specific incidence, compliance cost per firm, consumer pass-through, or whether a rule improves environmental or social outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Small exporters, agricultural producers, food-importing households and states, firms facing standards, regulators, workers, and communities exposed to climate and fertilizer shocks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Trade and environmental rules can improve safety, climate resilience, labor conditions, and transparency when designed with technical support and transition assistance; open trade alone does not guarantee food security.

related_sources.claim: Official UNCTAD PDF with the ten-trend trade update, services, South–South trade, food security, critical minerals, and regulation findings.
UNCTAD public summary of the ten trends and their geopolitical, digital, green, and regulatory framing.

boundary: This record adds a trade-system route from geopolitical fragmentation and regulation through value-chain relocation, services, South–South trade, food security, and compliance exposure. It is publication-level aggregate evidence, not firm-level causal analysis, household-price evidence, respondent data, or proof that trade openness or regulation produces inclusive welfare.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UNCTAD publication page, public ten-trend summary, and official PDF were reviewed; growth forecasts, value-chain share, services, South–South trade, discriminatory measures, technical regulations, food-export dependence, fertilizer, climate, and policy-direction claims were cross-checked.
